texto:
The local pack is the block Google places near the top of a search results page when a query suggests the searcher wants something nearby: a map with pins, followed by three business listings showing a name, star rating, review count, category, opening hours and buttons for directions, calls or the website. It exists because a large share of searches concern physical places, and a list of ten blue links answers "dentist" or "plumber near me" poorly. Google fills the block from Google Business Profile records and Maps data rather than from crawled web pages, which makes it a distinct ranking system with its own inputs, filters and, since 2016, its own advertising.
How the pack is assembled
The process begins with intent. Google decides whether a query has local intent, either explicitly ("pizza Leeds", "near me") or implicitly ("pharmacy", "car wash"), and whether a map belongs on the page. When it does, the system draws candidates from its places index, which Robby Stein, Google's vice-president of product for Search, put at 250 million places in October 2025. The three winners appear in the pack; a "more places" link opens the Local Finder, a longer list paired with a larger map.
Ranking rests on three inputs that Google has documented for years. Relevance measures how well a profile matches the query, which depends heavily on the primary category and the completeness of the record. Distance measures how far each business is from the searcher, or from the location named in the query; when neither is supplied, Google uses whatever it knows about the searcher's position. Prominence reflects how well known a business is, drawing on links, articles, directory listings and review counts. PPC Land summarised Google's documentation of the three factors in November 2024. As of October 2026 Google's help page describes local results as "mainly based on relevance, distance, and popularity", keeps prominence as a heading, and states: "There's no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google."
A filtering layer sits on top. When several listings appear to represent the same business, or businesses share a phone number, website or address, Google shows one and suppresses the rest. Practitioners detect filtering by zooming out the Local Finder map, which can reveal hidden listings. The most studied change to that filter, nicknamed Possum and observed from September 1, 2016, extended it to shared physical addresses, which hit law firms and medical practices in shared buildings hardest.
Advertising enters through location assets in Google Ads. Ads in the pack appear as listings labelled as sponsored, drawn from advertisers whose search campaigns carry a linked Business Profile address. Advertisers cannot buy the pack alone; clicks are reported as location details, directions or calls. Sponsored listings in the pack rose from under 3% of tracked mobile keywords in early November 2025 to about 22% in January 2026, according to Places Scout data covering 1,200 mobile ranking reports shared by the consultant Joy Hawkins.
From ten listings to three
Google blended local listings into its main results as a block of ten in January 2008, according to a history compiled by the local search analyst David Mihm, and cut the block to seven in October 2009. Places results were merged more fully into standard search in October 2010, months after the Local Business Center was renamed Google Places on April 20, 2010.
The modern format arrived in early August 2015. On August 7, 2015 Barry Schwartz of Search Engine Roundtable reported that Google was showing "only 3 local listings with a link to show more" instead of seven. Phone numbers, full addresses and Google+ links disappeared from the listings, while photos and opening hours were added. The industry quickly adopted "3-pack", sometimes "snack pack", for the result.
Monetisation followed within a year. At its Performance Summit on May 24, 2016, Google announced promoted pins in Maps and what it called the "next generation of local search ads", saying local searches on mobile were growing 50% faster than mobile searches overall, according to Search Engine Land.
Ranking changes were mostly inferred rather than announced. Pigeon on July 24, 2014 and Possum in 2016 were named by practitioners. Google confirmed a November 2019 local update that applied neural matching on December 2, 2019, its first acknowledged local ranking change. The update known as Vicinity, which rolled out between November 30 and December 8, 2021, was confirmed on December 16, 2021 as "a rebalancing of various factors we consider in generating local search results". The agency Sterling Sky, which named it, found that it raised the weight of proximity and reduced the benefit of stuffing keywords into business names. The same month, Google confirmed to Search Engine Land a desktop redesign moving the map to the right of the three listings.
Why it matters to marketers
For businesses that depend on footfall or phone calls, the pack often sits above every organic result, so ranking fourth carries a cost that ranking fourth in web search does not. For paid search teams, the pack's shift from purely organic to partly sponsored changes the calculation: a slot once won through categories and reviews can now be bought through location assets.
The pack is also becoming an input rather than only an output. PPC Land reported in April 2026 that profile records now feed Gemini, Ask Maps and Search, with Google's community newsletter claiming Ask Maps analyses data from 300 million places. The same categories, attributes and reviews that decide the three listings increasingly decide what a conversational answer recommends.
Where it fails and who disputes it
Fake listings are the oldest complaint. In June 2019 The Wall Street Journal estimated, from surveys of specialists, that roughly 11 million falsely listed businesses appeared on Google Maps on a typical day; Google replied that it had removed more than 3 million fake profiles in 2018. Google's 2025 Trust and Safety Report recorded more than 13 million fake Business Profiles removed and 292 million policy-violating reviews blocked or removed, alongside 79 million inaccurate edits.
Opacity is a second criticism. Google keeps the algorithm's details confidential, and its updates are often confirmed late or never. Danny Sullivan, Google's search liaison, called the failure to announce the 2021 update "a miss in this case".
Competition law questions whether the pack should exist in its current form. Yelp sued Google on August 28, 2024 in the Northern District of California, alleging that Google uses its general search monopoly to place its own local units above organic results regardless of quality. On June 30, 2026 Magistrate Judge Susan van Keulen barred Google from relitigating its monopoly power in general search, according to Courthouse News, leaving Yelp to prove abuse in local search. In Brussels, the European Commission's July 23, 2026 decision under the Digital Markets Act (DMA) named places intermediation and Google Maps among nine services, with a 460 million euro fine. Google has described such units as previews of search results rather than separate products, a position the consultancy Near Media called a material misrepresentation.
Not the same as
Google Maps. The standalone mapping product and app. Maps search uses the same places data but returns a full map of results and has its own ad formats, such as promoted pins; the pack is a block inside the Search results page.
Organic local results. The ordinary web links that appear below the pack for local queries, such as directory pages or a business's own site. They are ranked by Google's web search systems, not by the profile-based local algorithm.
Local Services Ads. A pay-per-lead format for trades and professional services, launched in 2015 as Home Service Ads, that runs in a separate unit with Google Verified badges. Its listings are not part of the three-pack, even when they appear on the same page.
Google Business Profile. The free listing that supplies data to the pack. A profile is the record; the pack is one place where records compete. Profile types such as the service-area business shape how distance is calculated.
Recent developments
Generative answers now sit beside the pack rather than replacing it. A Whitespark study by Miriam Ellis, published on May 12, 2025 and covering 540 queries in Houston, Phoenix and Denver, found local packs on 93% of queries with local intent and AI Overviews on 15% of them; for hybrid queries the ratio flipped, with AI Overviews on 97% and packs on 17%. That month Search Engine Roundtable reported a test, spotted by Chris Lonergan, in which an AI Overview replaced the pack for a "near me" query. AI-generated summaries also misfire: in July 2026 an AI Overview told searchers that Anna Mae's Bakery in Ontario was closing, confusing it with a bakery of the same name in Illinois.
Google's assistants are drawing on the same data. Gemini began serving local results from Maps in a visual format on December 13, 2025, without explaining how businesses are selected. Third parties benefit too: Yelp drew 512,680 citations in AI answers to local questions in the fourth quarter of 2025, about two thirds of them from Google's AI Mode. Users remain sceptical: only 15% of US adults trust AI search platforms "a lot", according to a Yelp and Morning Consult survey.
Paid inventory around the pack keeps expanding. Google opened Maps as a Demand Gen placement on May 20, 2026, and Local Services Ads began moving into Google Ads as a pay-per-lead Performance Max campaign type in August 2026, serving on Search and Maps in the same positions as before.

Summary
Who. Google designs and ranks the local pack and sells the sponsored listings within it. Businesses, agencies and listing-management vendors compete for its three slots through Google Business Profile, while practitioners such as Sterling Sky, BrightLocal and Whitespark track its behaviour. Yelp, the European Commission and a US federal court have examined Google's treatment of its local units.
What. A results block combining a map with three business listings, ranked on relevance, distance and prominence from Business Profile and Maps data, filtered for duplicates and, since the mid-2010s, partly sold through location assets.
When. Local listings were blended into Google results as a ten-listing block in January 2008, cut to seven in October 2009 and to three in August 2015. Ads arrived from 2016, and sponsored listings grew sharply between November 2025 and January 2026.
Where. Near the top of Google Search results on desktop and mobile for queries with local intent, with the Local Finder and Google Maps behind it, and increasingly alongside AI Overviews, AI Mode and Gemini.
Why. Searchers looking for nearby businesses want addresses, ratings and directions rather than web pages, and Google wants to supply them from its own data. The disputes follow from the same design: three slots concentrate traffic, reviews invite manipulation, and rivals argue that Google's own local units should not automatically sit above everyone else's.
